knownFor: A Persian Christian poet and teacher of Scripture who led the school of Edessa for twenty years, fled to Nisibis when accused of heresy and of siding with Persia, and founded there, with Barsauma of Nisibis, the school of the Church of the East.
datesNote: Left Edessa in 457 by R. H. Connolly's account, or after 471 if the bishop named by Barhadbeshabba stands, as François Nau notes; died in 502 by Connolly after Alphonsus Mingana, or in 503 or 504 by Nau's reckoning
role: Poet and head of the schools of Edessa and Nisibis

keyWorks.title: Metrical homilies
keyWorks.about: verse homilies on Scripture and the sacraments; Ebedjesu, a writer of the 1200s, credits him with 360, Connolly reports, and the Library holds four in Connolly's English

keyWorks.title: An Exposition of the Mysteries (Homily XVII)
keyWorks.about: a verse account of the eucharistic liturgy; late writers gave it to a writer of the 1200s, and Connolly argues it is Narsai's

keyWorks.title: On Baptism (Homily XXII)
keyWorks.about: a verse homily on baptism and anointing, in Connolly's English

traces: The Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, as R. H. Connolly translates it: "Edessa was darkened, but Nisibis shone forth". It names Narsai and his successors as the heads of the school of Nisibis.
Connolly writes that with the school of Nisibis began the formation of "what is now known as the Nestorian Church".
remembered: Mari ibn Sulayman, writing in the 1100s, reports that Theodulus, a disciple of Mar Diodore, blessed him and called him the tongue of the East and the poet of the Christian religion.
Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia tells his life as a saint's life, with the healing of a boy and a long fight against Satan.
Simeon of Beth Arsham, of the opposing side, calls him Narsai the leper, in a letter that Bar Hebraeus's editors quote from Assemani.

uncertain: His life comes almost wholly from Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia, who wrote in praise of the saints of his own church near the end of the 500s, by François Nau's dating. Mari ibn Sulayman and Bar Hebraeus wrote centuries later. François Nau gives the History to Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia, and the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools to Barhadbeshabba, bishop of Halwan in 605; he thinks it not impossible that they are one man.

When he left Edessa is disputed. Connolly gives 457, the year the followers of Ibas were expelled. Barhadbeshabba names a bishop of Edessa who took office in 471, Nau notes; Nau thinks an earlier bishop is meant, since otherwise Narsai would have left after 471 and died after 512. Addai Scher, editing the Cause, doubts that Narsai and his companions were expelled together in 457, as Simeon of Beth Arsham told it.

His years at Nisibis are told three ways: forty in Barhadbeshabba's History, forty-five in the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, and fifty in Bar Hebraeus. So his death is put in 502 by Connolly after Mingana, in 503 or 504 by Nau, and in 507 by those who follow Bar Hebraeus, as Nau reports.

Barhadbeshabba gives the quarrel with Barsauma to the jealousy of Barsauma's wife. Bar Hebraeus, hostile, says Barsauma expelled Narsai over a concubine. All three tellers say the two were reconciled.
That all his skill in Scripture came from Theodore of Mopsuestia rests on his homily on the three Doctors, as Connolly reports it; the Library does not hold that homily.

Connolly treats three of the four homilies he translates as certainly his. The Exposition of the Mysteries was given by one or two late authorities to a writer of the 1200s; Connolly argues it is Narsai's.

briefReferences: Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia, History of the holy Fathers, ch. XXXI, tr. François Nau (PO 9): born at Ma'alta in Persian territory; written at the end of the 500s, by Nau's dating, in praise of a saint of his own church.

History, tr. Nau: the charges at Edessa, a heretic who follows Theodore and Nestorius, his mind with the Persians, wanting to hand over the city; his refusal to agree outwardly; condemned to be burned, warned by a friend, his flight that night; the Persians at the city church who carried his books to Nisibis, for they were all his treasure.
History, tr. Nau: he meant to go east, into the middle of Persia, to teach; later two of his students denounced him to King Qawad as an enemy of his empire; forty years at Nisibis.

Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, tr. Addai Scher (PO 4): Narsai and Barsauma at the school of Edessa; Theodore's commentaries put into Syriac; Narsai head of the school for twenty years, giving commentaries with chant every day.

Cause, tr. Scher: Barsauma has him brought into the city with great honour, asks him to found a school and promises help; Persian and Syrian students come, and most of those at Edessa; the school's verdict, "Edessa grew dark; Nisibis grew bright"; forty-five years at Nisibis.
Cause, tr. Scher: the school founded by Bar-Sauma, bishop, and Rabban Narsai, priest; after him Elisha, then Abraham, a kinsman of Narsai.

Letter of Simeon of Beth Arsham, in J. S. Assemani's Latin (Bibliotheca Orientalis I) and as Bar Hebraeus's editors quote it: "Narses Leprosus"; the school at Edessa overthrown by the work of Bishop Cyrus and the order of the emperor Zeno.
Chronicle of Edessa, tr. Cowper, no. 73: in the year 800 of the Greeks (489) the school of the Persians was rooted out of Edessa.
Statutes of the School of Nisibis, ed. Ignazio Guidi, introduction: the first statutes, made in 496 while Narsai was its master; under Khosrau I the school swore to keep the canons of Narsai.
Bar Hebraeus, Ecclesiastical Chronicle III, tr. Abbeloos and Lamy: fifty years at Nisibis.
R. H. Connolly, The Liturgical Homilies of Narsai, note to Homily XXII: his enemies called him "The Leper", his friends "The Harp of the Holy Spirit".
Homily XXII (On Baptism), tr. Connolly: "As in a furnace He re-cast our image in Baptism".
World census, The Church of the East under Persia: his tradition, the Christians under the Persian shahs.

quotationOriginals.modern: Schools multiplied in the empire of the Persians. Edessa grew dark; Nisibis grew bright. The empire of the Romans filled with error, and that of the Persians with the knowledge of the fear of God.
quotationOriginals.printed: Les écoles se multiplièrent dans l'empire des Perses; Édesse s’obscurcit; Nisibe s’illumina: l'empire des Romains s’emplit d'erreur, celui des Perses de la connaissance de la crainte de Dieu.
quotationOriginals.work: Barhadbeshabba, Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, tr. Addai Scher (PO 4)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Scher's French; the Syriac OCR is unreadable. The printed wording joins Scher's line-break hyphen in "Ro- mains".

quotationOriginals.modern: In baptism he recast our image, as in a furnace. In place of our clay, he has made us spiritual gold.
quotationOriginals.printed: As in a furnace He re-cast our image in Baptism ; and instead of our clay He has made us spiritual gold.
quotationOriginals.work: Narsai, Homily XXII (On Baptism), tr. R. H. Connolly
